rows.claim: Barkley found that when time feels vague, you wait instead of starting.
Barkley found that wanting to start and being able to start are two different things.
Hallowell found that keeping every option open leaves you hovering over all of them.
Hallowell found that attention follows what interests you, not what matters most.
Cowan found the mind holds about four things at once. A longer list drops one.
Cowan found that adding a fifth thing pushes out the first, and you do not notice.
Leroy found that an unfinished job keeps taking a piece of your attention.
Leroy found that switching jobs costs you more than the time the switch takes.
Walker found that brief wakings are normal. The trouble starts when you worry about them.
Walker found that bright light in the evening pushes your sleep signal later.
Espie found that checking the clock turns a normal waking into a maths problem.
Espie found that trying harder to sleep makes sleep less likely.
LeDoux found the body reacts to a message before you have read it.
LeDoux found the mind practises for danger. That helps with a lion, not an email.
Nolen-Hoeksema found that going over it feels like solving it, and never is.
Nolen-Hoeksema found that going over a moment again lowers your mood instead of settling it.
Brewer found that a habit sticks when it makes you feel better, even briefly.
Brewer found that seeing what a habit gives you loosens it. Deciding to stop does not.
The Nagoskis found the body needs a clear sign that the hard part is over.
The Nagoskis found that the problem ending and your body settling are two separate things.
Emotional exhaustion stems from completing stress cycles without adequate recovery time.
Maslach found that if you measure yourself by output, stopping feels like slipping.
Maslach found that burnout comes from the job not fitting the person, not from weakness.
Tawwab found that every reason you give is one more thing to argue with.
Tawwab found that a limit tells someone about you. It is not a demand on them.
Lerner found that if no needs a reason, a one word answer becomes a court case.
Lerner found that changing your part makes people push back. That is not proof you were wrong.
People who suffer from overfunctioning often sacrifice their own needs to manage the lives of others.
Women trapped in overfunctioning often take responsibility for fixing their partner's emotional tasks.
Walker found that some people learn to keep everyone happy first, before anything else.
Walker found that keeping the peace becomes automatic, and starts before you decide to.
People-pleasing behaviors often stem from an unconscious fawn response to avoid potential interpersonal conflict.
Neff found that being kind to yourself helps you keep going. Being hard on yourself stops you.
Neff found it helps more to know other people struggle too than to blame yourself.
A self-compassion break helps individuals respond to suffering with kindness, not harsh self-judgment.
Clear found that every small action is a vote for the person you are becoming.
Clear found that shrinking the first step works better than growing the goal.
Gollwitzer found that saying when and where you will act roughly doubles the odds.
Gollwitzer found that an if then plan makes the moment decide for you.
Porges found that people used to unpredictable moods read a flat tone as a warning.
Porges found the body decides a room is safe before you have thought about it.
We choose emotional numbing as a way to avoid the vulnerability of our daily lives.
People internalize the relentless belief of being never enough when evaluating daily performance.
People struggling with codependency often prioritize others' needs while neglecting their own authentic desires.
Overcoming codependent patterns is essential for preventing exhaustion from over-giving and self-neglect.
The book describes caretaking behavior as an attempt to control others' lives and feelings.
Codependency describes losing self in another's problems, often leading to poor personal boundaries.
Some people meet fear by keeping other people happy, instead of fighting or leaving.
Chronic work stress leads directly to emotional exhaustion and depersonalization toward clients.
Chronic work stress leads directly to emotional exhaustion and detachment from clients.
Chronic work stress often triggers severe depersonalization toward clients and colleagues.
Fear, obligation, and guilt drive people into emotional blackmail when trying to please others.
Chronic compulsive caretaking stems from suppressing authentic needs to maintain attachment.
Nagoski describes feeling drained after caring too much for too long.
Brown links being open with others to love and a sense of belonging.
Tawwab says people cannot guess your boundaries from body language or what you leave unsaid.
Winter puts a steady wake time first when setting a sleep routine.
Hallowell describes a man whose focus kept breaking as small things drew him away from his task.
LeDoux says the brain's threat responses and feelings of fear work together, but are not the same.
